justification: This is a genuine original contribution to the target query, not a repackaging of the top results. Both comparison pages assert the flat 'value types live on the stack' claim as fact (Albahari: 'The stack is a simple first-in last-out memory structure, and is highly efficient,' presented without qualification as where value types live), and the official Microsoft Learn value-types page never even raises the stack/heap question at all — it only covers copy semantics. This article instead measures the claim with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread and produces six concrete counter-cases (a struct array that is 100% heap, a captured struct local that heap-allocates via a closure, a class instance the JIT keeps entirely off the heap via escape analysis), then explains all six with the correct underlying rule (placement follows lifetime, not the keyword) and backs it with Eric Lippert's 'stack is an implementation detail' argument and the Framework Design Guidelines. I fetched three of its non-obvious inline quotations against their live source pages (CS1612, the Records value-equality section, and the Choosing Between Class and Struct 2008-reprint notice/16-byte rule) and all three are verbatim-accurate and used in context — this is sourced correction, not contrarianism for its own sake. Web searches on five distinctive sentences ('placement follows lifetime, not the struct keyword,' 'a copy of an immutable value is indistinguishable from the original,' the Lippert paraphrase, etc.) turned up no matching or closely paraphrased passages elsewhere; the water-tank example, the Meter/Station defensive-copy demo and the boxing-cost measurement are original constructions. There is no filler intro/outro, no restated-title opening, no boilerplate 'Introduction'/'Conclusion' headings, and the nine section headings are all content-specific — a clear structural contrast with the generic phrasing typical of the top-ranking blog posts for this query. Exercises (4, within the required 3-6) vary in form (predict-the-output, find-the-bug, measure-it, extend-the-code) rather than repeating 'predict the output' each time, matching the brief's anti-template rule. The one real defect is that the 'Find the lost update' exercise prints its output ('40 60') directly under the problem statement instead of inside the collapsed solution, which is the exact 'giving away exercises' failure mode the editorial brief's binding pilot-round lessons call out and which cost earlier pilot articles their pass; the other three exercises on this page correctly withhold output until the solution. `node tools/run-code.mjs` passes (34 blocks, 19 executed), all cited docs and archived-blog sources resolve and support the sentences that cite them, and all glossary anchors used (value-type, reference-type, call-stack, garbage-collection) exist in src/content/glossary. This clears the 8.5 'equal to MDN/Real Python' anchor and approaches the 10 anchor (clearly better than the best existing result) on originality and rigor, held back from a higher score only by the one exercise-reveal defect.
